en: *The Method for Accomplishing Dream-Vision*, one fascicle,
composed by the Abhiṣeka Ācārya of the Translation Institute of Daxingshan Monastery (etc.).
Now, having opened and examined the essential texts of the Secret Treasury, I find herein the "Method for Accomplishing Dream-Vision," intended for the sake of sentient beings in the final age.
Regarding these sequential ritual procedures: within a clean room, construct a square altar of any size according to one's preference.
Upon that altar, prepare the various offering substances, namely: incense, flowers, oil lamps, food and drink, cakes, ghee, honey, *modaka* (joy-balls), and so forth.
Such a variety cannot be fully described; use whatever fresh items are available at the time.
Next, the ritual for the Request is stated as follows:
I now request the Buddha-Eyed Honored One, Mañjuśrī, and the wondrous bannered assembly of attendants,
the Seven Stars of the Big Dipper, the Nine Planets, and so forth, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and the twelve zodiacal signs.
The twelve heavenly kings and the twelve divine generals, The various nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others,
The kings of mountains, the kings of rivers, and the great tree kings— All the great benevolent deities of the ten directions,
Not transgressing the power of our sincere invitation, Please descend to this site and accept these sublime offerings.
Protect so-and-so and dispel all inauspiciousness; Fulfill auspicious dreams and all aspirations.
Next, the Great Hook-Summoning Mantra is recited: (Form the inner-bind mudrā and beckon with the right wind.)
Homage to Akṣobhyatathāgatasya guṇasamudayeśvaraprabhūṣaṇāya svāhā!
If there are sentient beings who recite this mantra, all the assemblies of noble ones— devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas— all shall follow with joy and come.
[He] approaches.
Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishing auspicious dreams, one should pay homage to the North and form this thought:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha; [I take refuge in] Mañjuśrī, the Wondrous Banner, and the Great Dipper Star."
The twelve Heavenly Kings and the various lunar mansions perceive auspicious dreams and fulfill one's aspirations.
Furthermore, the mantra is recited as follows: Oṃ āve ra hūṃ khajraḥ.

If there are sentient beings who have seen auspicious dreams but are unable to achieve their fulfillment, they should, by means of this teaching, recollect Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva Subhadhvaja, and others.
If they recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while lying down, they will always obtain auspicious dreams and be able to know matters of good and evil.
If anyone obtains an auspicious dream and wishes to bring it to fulfillment, they should perform empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If one eats [the food] seven times, one will attain accomplishment before long, with the sole exception of dreams arising from anxious thoughts.
Furthermore, as for the method for anyone who wishes to eliminate bad dreams: one should pay homage to the direction of the Northern Dipper and form this thought:
I now take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, In Mañjuśrī, Subhūṣaṇadhvaja, the Big Dipper, the twelve celestial kings, and all the lunar mansions.
May evil dreams be dispelled and auspicious matters be attained.
Furthermore, the mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ śrī-kālarūpa hūṃ khaṃ svāhā.

If any sons or daughters of good family should encounter bad dreams or the appearance of inauspicious omens, they should fashion a human figure out of *mita* wood, write that mantra upon it, and empower it seven times for three consecutive days;
finally, that human figure should be placed [in the appropriate location].
In mountain forests and by great rivers, inauspiciousness is extinguished and the mind becomes peaceful and joyful.
If someone constantly obtains auspicious dreams, even one who does not practice in this way will not fail to achieve accomplishment for long;

even if inauspicious signs are extinguished, though one may see bad dreams, such a practitioner should not fail to have their affairs turn auspicious again. Furthermore, take white thread to make a cord and recite the mantra twenty times.
One should not experience three types of evil dreams while bound by fetters in the body during inhalation or exhalation.
Furthermore, the mantra for making offerings is spoken as follows: (Vajra-palms joined, with the two *vāyu* fingers in the shape of a jewel).
Oṃ amoghapūjā-maṇipradīpa-namovākye tathāgatavilokite samantaprasara hūṃ.
If there are sentient beings who recite this mantra while making offerings to the Triple Gem, immeasurable clouds of offerings will flow forth.
One makes offerings to the entire assembly of noble ones with the ocean [of offerings].

Furthermore, the mantra for bestowing food is as follows: (With the right hand, rub the *ākāśa* finger against the *tejas* nail three or two times; extend the remaining three fingers; then, snap the *vāyu* finger against the *ākāśa* finger to produce a sound, snapping once for each recitation, seven times in total).
*Namo sarvatathāgatavajriṇe oṃ svabhara svabhara hūṃ.* If there is anyone who,
having empowered food and drink with this mantra, bestows it upon all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, etc.,
mountain kings, ocean kings, river kings, great tree kings, and all spirits and deities, each and every one of them...
They obtained seventy-seven *dronas* of food, the standard measure used in the kingdom of Magadha, and were all completely satiated.
Next, he dispatched them with this verse:
"May the Noble Assembly, together with all their retinues, bestow their blessings upon [Name]."
*Hanki daikyū jōju mōshōhō* (The Return to the Great Palace:
The Accomplishment of the Dream-Visualization Method), one fascicle.
Copied on the eighteenth day of the first month of the sixth year of Hōen; the *yiten* (revised punctuation) was applied.

On the third day of the sixth month in the first year of Karoku, I received [this text] at the ritual site in Horikawa while attending the chamber of the Sōjō (Archbishop) Nikkōbō; it was recorded by Enjun.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the first year of Bun’ei, I transcribed it; it was recorded by Jikan.
On the same day, the eleventh of the seventh month, I received [this text] from the presence of the venerable Sōgū of Shugetsudō; it is recorded as completed.
On the eighteenth of the same month, I compared it with various manuscripts and added ink marks for verification.
